title: Stapleton’s analogies: moral/hope certainty of pardon without faith-certainty or endless fluctuation
source_text: XXIII. Similia docet Thomas Stapletonus, lib. 9. de Justif. cap. 11. Quemadmodum, inquit, qui legitime certat, certo credit se coronandum; & qui filius est primogenitus, patris haeredem se futurum; & qui itineri se commitit, se ad finem salvum perventurum; denique ut omnis Christianus certo credit se infantem baptizatum fuisse & esse, qui filius matris suae quae dicitur filium se esse? & tamen nihil horum certitudine fidei habetur, sed solum certitudine, partim spei & fiduciae bonae, partim morali; sic de remissione peccatorum & gratia Dei certo credere potest se eam esse consecutum, qui quae Deus praecipit ad ea consequenda sese praestitisse sibi conscius est: nec tamen, vel certitudine fidei idem credere potest, aut debet: vel quia talem certitudinem non habet, propterea, incertus, anceps, aut dubius est, aut per modum fluctuantis se habet. Talis enim ut describit Jacobus, similis est fluctui maris, qui a vento movetur & circumfertur. Nec ergo Protestantium extremam sententiam, (quae est certitudo fidei excludens omnem formidinem & timorem propriae indispositionis, cum securitate illa qualis huic peregrinationi non competit); nec animi perpetuo suspensi fluctuationem incertam & inconstantem, quae huc illucque momento impellitur, docent Catholici circa remissionem peccatorum aut praesentem justitiam; sed mediam sententiam docent: quae est certitudo spei ex parte promissionum divinarum firmissima, & certitudo, vel conjecturalis, vel etiam moralis, ex parte propriae dispositionis, cujus quisque sibi conscius est, qui legitime dispositus est: quae sane utraque & omnem dubitationem in sensu Protestantium, id est, qua neutri parti assentitur excludit, & firmam conscientiis pacem & consolationem affert contra omnes luctas tentationum, vel diffidentiae, vel pusillanimitatis, vel denique desperabundae dubitationis.
pass_a_gloss: Thomas Stapleton teaches similar things in On Justification, book 9, chapter 11. Just as, he says, he who lawfully contends certainly believes he will be crowned; and he who is a firstborn son that he will be his father’s heir; and he who commits himself to a journey that he will arrive safe at the end; finally as every Christian certainly believes that he was and is a baptized infant, who is a son of his mother who is said to be a son?—and yet none of these is held with the certainty of faith, but only with a certainty partly of good hope and trust, partly moral; so concerning the remission of sins and the grace of God he can certainly believe that he has obtained it who is conscious to himself that he has performed what God commands for obtaining those things: and yet neither can or ought he believe the same with the certainty of faith; nor because he does not have such certainty is he therefore uncertain, double-minded, or doubtful, or does he behave in the manner of one fluctuating. For such a one, as James describes, is like a wave of the sea moved and carried about by the wind. Therefore Catholics teach neither the extreme opinion of the Protestants (which is a certainty of faith excluding every fear and dread of one’s own indisposition, with that security which does not belong to this pilgrimage), nor an uncertain and inconstant fluctuation of a mind perpetually suspended, which is driven hither and thither in a moment, concerning the remission of sins or present righteousness; but they teach a middle opinion: which is a most firm certainty of hope on the side of the divine promises, and a certainty, either conjectural or even moral, on the side of one’s own disposition, of which each is conscious to himself who is lawfully disposed—which two together both exclude every doubt in the Protestants’ sense, that is, that by which assent is given to neither side, and bring firm peace and consolation to consciences against all struggles of temptations, whether of distrust, or of pusillanimity, or finally of despairing doubt.
pass_b_english: Stapleton compares assurance of pardon to certainty of crowning, inheritance, safe travel, or one’s baptism—moral/hope certainty, not faith-certainty.
Catholics claim a middle path: firm hope on the promises plus dispositional signs, without Protestant absolute security or endless fluctuation.
